chunks.document_content: Allocation Anti-VEGF combined with retinal laser photocoagulation ac-counted for 45.65% of the main combination regimens. Anti-VEGF drugs (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) rapidly reduce macular edema and inhibit neovascular activity by neutralizing VEGF, with a fast onset but limited duration of action. Laser photocoagulation, by contrast, destroys high oxygen-consuming photoreceptor cells to reduce retinal ischemia and hypoxia, thereby decreasing sustained VEGF production; it offers durable efficacy but a slower onset. Seminal trials, including the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) and DRCR.net Protocol I, have established the evidence base for current management strat-egies: ETDRS defined diagnostic criteria and laser standards, while Protocol I validated combination therapy efficacy. Anti-VEGF combined with glucocorticoids may benefit patients who respond poorly to anti-VEGF therapy alone, but the adverse effects such as increased intraocular pressure and accelerated cataract progression limit their widespread use. The current main treatment regimen for CI-DME/PDR is centered on anti-VEGF therapy, with individual-ized plans optimized based on patient-specific conditions. Future research should focus on optimizing combination regimen timing, identifying suitable patient populations, the exploration of novel combination strategies (34). The sample sizes of diabetic retinopathy studies are generally small - 61.81% enrolled fewer than 100 participants, with studies of 1-50 participants being the most common (39.18%), while large-scale trials with over 300 participants accounted for only 13.15%. This scarcity of adequately powered studies is partly attributable to the relatively small PDR patient pool at individual centers, making it difficult for single sites to accrue more than 100 cases (36). Small samples compromise statistical power and increase the risk of type II errors, thereby undermining both internal validity and reproduc-ibility of reported treatment effects. The establishment of multicen-ter collaborative networks, such as the DRCR.net series (Protocol I/ T/V), RESTORE, RESOLVE, and VISTA/VIVID, is therefore es-sential not only to increase enrollment capacity but also to ensure sufficient power for detecting clinically meaningful effects and to enhance the generalizability of findings across diverse populations (37). Future trials should prespecify minimum sample size calcula-tions based on clinically relevant effect sizes and incorporate interim power analyses where appropriate. Age standards are primarily focused on adults, consistent with normal research patterns. Gender standards did not impose restrictions, reflecting good awareness of external validity. Only one study was limited to males. Overall, reporting on the gender dimension is relatively standardized, but subsequent analyses should still pay attention to efficacy differences in gender subgroups. Baseline CRT values in women are usually lower than in men, which may affect the diagnostic threshold for DME and the assessment of treatment response. The United States demonstrated a strong emphasis on anti-VEGF therapies, with a total of 69 studies (47 trial registrations and 22 publications) indexed in PubMed. In contrast, China showed a predominant focus on perioperative interventions, with a total of 40 studies (35 trial registrations and 5 publications in PubMed). These findings suggest that geographical regions may have specific prior-ities in therapeutic strategies, accompanied by varying rates of translation from registration to publication. Intervention timing is mostly individualized, often without fixed treatment numbers and frequencies.

chunks.document_content: The role of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR/ErbB1) in diabetic retinopathy and its therapeutic implications Clinically, DM is classified into at least four categories, namely Type 1 (T1DM), Type 2 (T2DM), gestational diabetes, and other types arising from specific identi­ fiable causes [1]. In T1DM, an autoimmune response destroys insulin-producing β-cells in the pancreas, lead­ ing to an absolute insulin deficiency [1, 2]. In contrast, T2DM begins with insulin resistance of primarily skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and the liver, followed by a pro­ gressive, nonautoimmune decline in pancreatic β-cell function and insulin secretion [1]. Uncontrolled chronic hyperglycemia in both T1DM and T2DM can lead to a range of macrovascular and microvascular complications including cardiovascular [3], renal [4], neuronal [5], and retinal pathologies [6]. In addition to chronic hyperglyce­ mia, the classical risk factors for diabetes complications include smoking, dyslipidemias and hypertension [7]. to chronic retinal ischemia which results in prolifera­ tive diabetic retinopathy (PDR) [18]. At this stage, visual alterations are significantly more pronounced where damage to the retinal blood vessels is more severe, stimu­ lating the growth of new abnormal blood vessels (neovas­ cularization) through the process of angiogenesis [18]. This occurs through the upregulation of growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), both of which are expressed in response to hypoxia and are known to pro­ mote neovascularization [19, 20]. Additionally, diabetic macular edema (DME) is a common complication of both NPDR and PDR, where the blood-retinal-barrier (BRB) is compromised with increased vascular permeability cul­ minating in fluid accumulation in the macula, the central region of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed vision [14]. DME is a common cause of visual impairment in DR patients [18]. ​Introduction Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is a group of chronic endocrine diseases characterized by persistent hyperglycemia [1]. The current standard of care for DR centers on intra­ vitreal anti-VEGF therapy, with agents such as bevaci­ zumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting VEGF-A [21]. Among various other inflammatory mediators, VEGF plays a central role in promoting both neovasculariza­ tion and vascular leakage in PDR [20]. Under hyperglyce­ mic and hypoxic conditions, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) upregulates VEGF expression which drives angiogenesis via ligand binding and downstream sig­ naling [22]. By sequestering VEGF and/or inhibiting its receptor signaling, these agents decrease fluid extravasa­ tion, resolve edema, and inhibit angiogenesis associated with PDR in the optic disc, retina and iris [23]. This review focuses on diabetic retinopathy (DR), the primary microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading cause of new cases of blindness among adults aged 20-74 years in developed countries [6, 7]. Approxi­ mately one-third of individuals with diabetes develop DR [8]. Its prevalence correlates strongly with both disease duration and glycemic control, as maintaining near-nor­ moglycemia can delay or prevent its onset and progres­ sion [7]. However, recent studies have also suggested that intensive therapies that result in rapid reductions in Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C), such as with glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, can be associated with initial worsening of DR at least in the early stages but may ultimately be protective in late or advanced stages [9-12].

Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), as one of the most com­ mon microvascular complications of diabetes, affects approximately 34.6% of individuals living with dia­ betes, with 30% progressing to varying degrees of vis­ ual impairment (Wang et al., 2024). The pathological characteristics primarily include capillary degener­ ation, loss of pericytes, and vessel leakage (Liu et al., 2023). At present, the therapeutic strategies for DR mainly focus on systemic treatment, vitrectomy, ret­ inal photocoagulation, and intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF inhibitors (Yamato et al., 2024). While these treatments primarily address advanced DR, their efficacy is limited for early-stage disease. They can also result in many adverse reactions, including pos­ sible permanent loss of peripheral vision and worsen­ ing macular edema (Hu et al., 2024). Exposure to high glucose and oxidative stress triggers reactive activation of ret­ inal microglia, accompanied by enhanced secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1b, IL-6, and TNF-a. chunks.document_content: Materials and methods Diabetic retinopathy (DR) has long been assessed primarily as a microangiopathy. However, recent studies have proposed the con-cept of diabetic retinal disease (DRD), which recognizes that retinal pathology involves not only the vascular system but also neural and glial cells and their interactions within the neurovascular unit (2, 3). This concept has increased interest in preclinical and early clinical signs of DRD to better understand the mechanisms and timing of disease onset (2). Both basic and clinical studies have demonstrated subtle but clear functional and structural changes in retinal neural tissue in diabetes (4-8). To analyze these early changes, we have been studying diabetic eyes at a stage before visible macular changes are detectable on fundus photographs and before the development of secondary changes associated with PDR and/or exudative fluid in DME (9, 10). However, their associations with systemic biomarkers have not yet been addressed, although diabetic complications tend to be associated not only with hyperglycemia but also with broader systemic metabolic alterations. Participants Non-invasive ocular imaging systems, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA), can detect subtle changes at the micrometer scale and are now widely used in clinical practice. OCT enables measurement not only of the thick-ness of the neural retinal layers but also of photoreceptor outer segment (PROS) length. Length of the PROS, where visual pigments are concentrated and act as light receptors, has been reported to be reduced in eyes with diabetes than in control (10), and as a marker of photoreceptor condition in eyes at high risk of age-related macular degeneration (11, 12). The volume of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a highly metabolic single-cell layer essential for photoreceptor maintenance, can also be measured on OCT images. Eye examinations The patients underwent ophthalmic examinations, including measurement of BCVA, intraocular pressure (IOP), and axial length, and acquisition of fundus photographs (California, Optos, Inc., MA), sectional and three-dimensional spectral-domain OCT images (Spectralis OCT, Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Dossenheim, Germany), and 3 x 3 mm OCT angiography (OCTA) (OCT HS-100; Canon, Inc., Tokyo, Japan) images. chunks.document_content: OPEN ACCESS EDITED BY Martina Tomic ́, Merkur University Hospital, Croatia RECEIVED 07 August 2026 REVISED 27 September 2026 ACCEPTED 29 September 2026 PUBLISHED 09 October 2026 Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy interventional trials: a scoping review on trial design, execution, and reporting practices Zixuan Wang 1, Xuwei Liu 2, Ming Yang 3, Guanchi Yan 3, Xuechun Fan 1, Jing Yu 3, Jinyue Zhao 3, Yingjing Shi 4* and Xi Chen 3* 1College of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun, China, 2School of Environment and Energy, Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture, Beijing, China, 3The Affiliated Hospital to Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun University of Chinese Medicine, Changchun, China, 4Changchun Disabled Persons Rehabilitation Center, Changchun, China CITATION Wang Z, Liu X, Yang M, Yan G, Fan X, Yu J, Zhao J, Shi Y and Chen X (2026) Mapping the methodological framework of diabetic retinopathy interventional trials: a scoping review on trial design, execution, and reporting practices. Front. Endocrinol. 17:1961622. doi: 10.3389/fendo.XXX-XXX-XXXX Background: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is a prevalent and sight-threatening ocular complication of diabetes, and one of the leading causes of vision loss and blindness among the working-age population worldwide. Driven by a growing understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying DR, treatment strategies have evolved from a sole focus on glycemic control to comprehensive, multi-targeted, and multimodal therapies. This study systematically summarizes the characteristics of current clinical trials focused on DR treatment and evaluates the employed research methodologies. The aim of this review is to explore methodological trends in specific domains, with the hope that such insights may inform future efforts to optimize trial design and improve trial quality. Methods: This study followed the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) were retrieved. In addition, clinical trials indexed in PubMed from July 23, 2016 to July 23, 2026 were retrieved. Data from the included studies were extracted and presented in tabular form. Results: Clinical research targeting DR has expanded rapidly, reflecting a shift toward diverse interventions like anti-Vascular endothelial growth factor(anti-VEGF) drugs, laser treatments, and combined therapies. However, several methodological limitations were noted in the included studies, including the failure to specify diabetes type in over half of the cases, a predominance of small-sample trials, inconsistent reporting of intervention duration, and limited implementation of blinding due to practical constraints in ophthalmic interventions. Functional outcomes were defined as measures of visual function, primarily best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). Anatomical outcomes were defined as structural measures of retinal morphology assessed by optical coherence tomography (OCT), including central retinal thickness (CRT), central macular thickness (CMT), intraretinal fluid (IRF), and subretinal fluid (SRF). thereby providing researchers with a structured reference to better inform future trial design. Prior research in this domain has predominantly centered on screening strategies and outcome pre-diction (25, 26). To date, however, no systematic review has specifically examined the methodological and design characteristics of interventional clinical trials for diabetic retinopathy. To our knowledge, the present study therefore constitutes the first com-prehensive assessment of diabetic retinopathy clinical trial features. Clinical research on diabetic retinopathy began to show an upward trend around 2005, coinciding with the emergence of the anti-VEGF therapeutic era. Following FDA approval of bevacizumab for oncological indications in 2004 and ranibizumab for neovascular age-related macular degeneration in 2006, the ophthalmology community rapidly initiated exploratory intravitreal injection studies. This paradigm shift fundamentally transformed DR/DME treatment, where laser photocoagulation had previously been the sole standard of care (27).This therapeutic shift stimulated substan-tial clinical investigations into the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens of anti-VEGF agents. Concurrently, the progressive adop-tion of optical coherence tomography (OCT) provided a standard-ized tool for objective quantitative assessment of retinal thickness, lowering the imaging threshold for clinical trials and further contributing to research growth (28). Between 2005 and 2017, DR clinical research maintained steady growth driven by landmark multicenter trials from the DRCR.net (e.g., Protocol I in 2012 establishing ranibizumab plus laser as standard DME therapy, and Protocol T in 2015 comparing ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab) (29, 30). chunks.document_content: OPEN ACCESS *CORRESPONDENCE Jing Chen RECEIVED 24 August 2026 REVISED 21 September 2026 ACCEPTED 25 September 2026 PUBLISHED 05 October 2026 Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a preventable cause of vision loss as diabetes prevalence rises worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled retinal screening has progressed from retrospective validation to prospective and real-world deployment, with recent reviews showing high diagnostic performance across fundus photography, smartphone-based systems, and autonomous platforms. Yet diagnostic accuracy alone does not ensure public health benefit. Population impact can be lost when eligible people are not reached, images are ungradable, results are delayed, referrals are incomplete, treatment capacity is insufficient, or disadvantaged groups face financial, geographic, or digital barriers. Unlike reviews centered mainly on diagnostic accuracy or economic performance, this Mini Review reframes AI-enabled DR screening as a population-health intervention spanning detection through completion of effective eye care. We synthesize evidence on diagnostic validity, implementation, economics, referral completion, care cascades, patient-centered outcomes, equity, and governance. We argue that effectiveness and cost-effectiveness are properties of the complete screening-to-treatment pathway, not the algorithm alone, and propose a four-domain framework encompassing technical validity, service integration, population impact, and equity and sustainability. Future research should prioritize comparative implementation studies and outcome sets that capture screening reach, gradability, referral completion, treatment initiation, time to treatment, avoidable vision loss, vision-related quality of life, acceptability, costs, and subgroup equity. The policy question is no longer whether AI can detect DR, but whether health systems can translate automated detection into equitable completion of effective eye care at scale. The public health challenge is expanding as diabetes prevalence rises: the International Diabetes Federation estimates that 589 million adults were living with diabetes in 2024, with projections approaching 853 million by 2050 (2). Updated global estimates suggest that more than 100 million adults already have DR, and the number is expected to increase substantially by 2045 (3). In this context, screening is not simply an ophthalmic service; it is a population-level strategy that links chronic disease management, primary care, imaging infrastructure, referral pathways, and timely treatment (4).

Nevertheless, many existing evaluations have focused primarily on factual cor­ rectness, readability, or overall response quality, and relatively few have integrated safety, patient-centered communication, struc­ tured information-quality measures, transparency, and readability within a single DR-focused evaluation. Consequently, existing evidence does not fully characterize how publicly accessible LLM interfaces perform across the multiple dimensions relevant to patient-facing DR education. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most common microvas­ cular complications of diabetes and remains a leading cause of pre­ ventable vision impairment among working-age adults worldwide. A global meta-analysis estimated that 22.3% of individuals with diabetes have DR and 6.2% have vision-threatening DR, corresponding to approximately 103 million affected adults in 2020 and a projected increase to 160 million by 2045 (1). Much of the vision loss associated with DR is potentially preventable through timely retinal screening, systemic risk-factor control, appropriate referral, and evidence-based treatment (2, 3). However, early DR is frequently asymptomatic, and the effectiveness of prevention depends partly on whether individuals understand screening recommendations, attend follow-up examina­ tions, and seek timely care after abnormal findings or new visual symptoms. People living with diabetes therefore require accessible and understandable health education regarding screening intervals, warn­ ing symptoms, treatment options, pregnancy-related risks, and long-term self-management. To address this gap, we conducted a CHART-aligned comparative evaluation of six widely accessible LLM interfaces-ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Doubao, Microsoft Copilot, and Perplexity-using 50 stan­ dardized patient-oriented DR questions (15). Unlike evaluations cen­ tered on a narrower set of outcomes, the present study combined guideline-based Safety and Accuracy assessment with Empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, Global Quality Score, and six readability metrics. This multidimensional, time-stamped design was intended to characterize how publicly accessible interfaces perform across the informational, communicative, safety, transpar­ ency, and readability dimensions relevant to patient-facing DR educa­ tion. Rather than establishing a permanent model ranking, the study identifies strengths, trade-offs, and areas that warrant evaluation before LLM-generated information is incorporated into routine patient education. Patients increasingly seek health information online, and con­ versational artificial intelligence systems are becoming readily accessible sources of patient-facing medical information (4). Large language models (LLMs) are emerging not only as question-answering technologies but also as digital health information sources and population-facing health communication channels. Their immediate and conversational responses may help address unmet information needs, particularly for chronic conditions that require repeated health education. However, LLM-generated information may also influence how users understand disease risk, interpret symptoms, and make decisions about screening and care-seeking. Responses that provide inaccurate screening inter­ vals, inadequate urgent-care advice, unrealistic treatment expecta­ tions, or unclear boundaries between AI-assisted screening and professional evaluation could contribute to delayed or inappropri­ ate care. Information that is technically accurate but excessively difficult to read may also be inaccessible to individuals with lim­ ited health literacy. This concern is particularly relevant because ophthalmic patient-education materials frequently exceed recom­ mended readability levels (5, 6).

Table 1 details the characteristics of the study populations. 3.4 Study population and basic characteristics of diabetic retinopathy Among the 707 studies, over half (364 studies, 51.49%) did not specify the type of diabetes, referring to it only in general terms. Of those that did, 245 studies (34.65%) distinguished between type 1 and type 2 diabetes; separately, 88 studies (12.45%) focused exclusively on type 2 diabetes, while only 10 (1.41%) were limited to type 1 diabetes. 3.5 Basic characteristics of clinical trials Regarding DR classification, PDR was the most frequently studied stage (197 studies, 27.86%), followed by NPDR (136 studies, 19.24%). Macular edema was a key feature in 51.63% of studies (365 studies), with Center-involved Diabetic Macular Edema (CI-DME) being the most specified subtype (208 studies, 29.42%). The included studies were predominantly small, with 61.81% enrolling fewer than 100 participants. Studies with 1-50 partici-pants were the most common (39.18%), followed by those with 51- 100 participants (22.63%). Large-scale trials with over 300 partic-ipants accounted for only 13.15%. Most studies (89.96%) established clear ophthalmic examina-tion criteria. However, fewer specified glycemic control criteria (25.32%) or ancillary examinations (27.58%).
